intro: “Träumerei” (Dreaming), No. 7 of Kinderszenen, Op. 15, stands at the centre of the set. It is twenty-four written bars long, and its quiet piano melody repeatedly rises a little higher.

sections.label: A · The opening eight bars repeated
A′ · F major, closing section
sections.mNote: A high A is held under a fermata before the close.

cues.title: Opening phrase, bars 1–4
cues.text: A single C rises to F and is held. The melody then climbs again towards the F an octave above. Underneath, the other voices move slowly, each with its own line.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, p. 11, bars 1–4; pitches confirmed in Ying-Chun Liu’s Mutopia transcription. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/fe/IMSLP03060-Schumann-Op015Brt6016.pdf
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Diary entries, 24–25 February 1838
cues.text: On Saturday, 24 February 1838, Schumann recorded in his diary that he had composed “the little thing Träumerei”. The following evening he worked on another Kinderszene, in F major, which he thought “very pretty”.
cues.evidence: Schumann’s diary, 24–25 February 1838, quoted in Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 1. Translations of “das kleine Ding” and “die mir sehr hübsch vorkommt”. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

cues.title: Letter to Clara Wieck, 1838
cues.text: On 17 March 1838 Schumann told Clara that he had written “some thirty small droll things” and chosen about twelve for his Kinderszenen. He promised that she would enjoy them, though she would have to forget herself as a virtuoso.
cues.evidence: Schumann to Clara Wieck, Leipzig, 17 March 1838, Jugendbriefe (1885), p. 277, quoted in Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 3: “an die 30 kleine putzige Dinger … von denen ich etwa zwölf ausgelesen”; our translation. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf Same letter, same sentences, in May Herbert’s English translation, Early Letters of Robert Schumann (1888), pp. 264–265: “about thirty quaint little things, from which I have selected twelve”. https://archive.org/details/earlylettersofro010823mbp

cues.title: Early programmes, Dresden and Vienna
cues.text: When Marie Wieck played six of the pieces in Dresden on 18 January 1853, Träumerei was not among them. In Vienna on 17 March 1857 Clara’s pupil Nanette Falk played three, all from Marie’s list, so it was missing from that programme too.
cues.evidence: Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), items 15 and 16: the Dresden programme of 18 January 1853 and the Vienna programme of 17 March 1857. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

cues.title: Return of the opening, bar 17
cues.text: After the middle passage’s cadences in G minor and D minor, the opening F returns at bar 17 and Schumann restores the first phrase. A high A is held under a fermata in bar 22. The final descent is marked ritardando.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 11, bars 9–24: G-minor and D-minor cadences, return at bar 17, fermata on A in bar 22 and final ritardando.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Illustrated editions and a film
cues.text: In 1877 Friederike Medem published silhouettes with verses for four of the pieces, Träumerei among them. A Leipzig edition of 1886 paired the music with poems by Albert Träger and pictures by Alexander Zick. In 1943–44 UFA made a film called Träumerei.
cues.evidence: Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), items 17, 33–34 and 38: the Zick and Träger edition, the UFA film Träumerei and the Medem silhouettes. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

transitions.title: Bar 8 into the repeat
transitions.to: A · The opening eight bars repeated
transitions.how: The music slows in the eighth bar onto C major harmony, the dominant of F. A low C in the melody becomes the upbeat back to F, while the bass moves beneath it to F. The repeat begins with the same upward figure as the opening.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 11, bar 8 and the repeat to bar 1; final C-major harmony confirmed in the Mutopia transcription.

transitions.title: The climb reaches E♭
transitions.from: A · The opening eight bars repeated
transitions.how: The new phrase begins on F over an F bass, as at the opening. Its climb now reaches E♭ in bar 10, and the inner parts move towards G minor, with a cadence in that key at bar 12. In bar 13 the rising shape begins again on B♭, with B♭ in the bass.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 11, bars 9–14; E♭ at bar 10, G-minor cadence at bar 12 and B♭ phrase at bar 13.

transitions.title: Return from D minor to F
transitions.how: The middle phrase comes to rest in D minor and slows. A grace-note C leads up to the opening F, and a low F in the bass beneath it restores the home key. The first phrase of the tune begins again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 11, bars 16–17; grace note and bass pitches checked against the Mutopia transcription.

composer.epithet: Composer and music critic, a bookseller’s son, whose piano music depicts lovers, masks and arguments.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The novels contain twins, disguises, and conversations that wander from their subject and return to it unexpectedly. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828 and moved to Heidelberg the following year. In the end he persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil and had more ground to make up. By 1832 paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and turned to composing and writing.
